title: The CLR & .NET Runtime
summary: .NET's answer to the JVM: Intermediate Language, assemblies, and RyuJIT. Learn the CLR's shape by contrasting it directly against the JVM concepts you just saw, and where the two runtimes genuinely diverge.

slides.markdown:
Everything `the-jvm-deep-dive` taught generalizes better than you'd expect — the **Common Language Runtime (CLR)**, .NET's managed runtime, has a bytecode format, a JIT, and a GC that map almost one-to-one onto JVM concepts, with different names and a few real differences.

C#, F#, and VB.NET all compile to the same intermediate format and run on the same CLR — the multi-language story the JVM only partially has (via the JVM bytecode target for Kotlin/Scala/Clojure). This topic builds the CLR by direct comparison: what plays the JVM's role, and where the two runtimes actually diverge, not just rename things.

slides.subTitle: .NET's class files and bytecode
slides.markdown:
An **assembly** (a `.dll` or `.exe`) is .NET's unit of deployment — roughly the JVM's JAR, but it also carries **metadata** (type info, versioning) directly inside itself, which is why .NET assemblies are largely self-describing without a separate manifest file the way older JAR conventions needed one.

**Intermediate Language (IL)**, also called MSIL or CIL, is the bytecode assemblies contain — the direct analog of a `.class` file's bytecode from `bytecode-and-virtual-machines`. Like JVM bytecode, IL is stack-based: the same push-operands-then-operate pattern you saw in `iload_1; iload_2; iadd` shows up as IL's `ldarg`/`add` sequence.

The practical payoff of a shared IL target: C#, F#, and VB.NET code can call each other directly and even inherit across languages, because they all compile down to the exact same IL and run on the exact same CLR.
![C# source compiled by Roslyn to IL, then JIT-compiled by RyuJIT to native machine code, with F# and VB.NET joining at the IL stage](assets/csharp-to-il-to-native.svg)

assets.alt: C# source compiled by Roslyn to IL, then JIT-compiled by RyuJIT to native machine code, with F# and VB.NET joining at the IL stage

slides.markdown:
**RyuJIT** is .NET's JIT compiler, and it tiers the same way HotSpot does, for the same reason: compile fast now, compile better once you know it's worth it.

- **Tier 0 (quick JIT)** — compiles a method almost immediately on first call, minimal optimization, fast to produce, with instrumentation added to gather call counts.
- **Tier 1 (optimized)** — recompiles methods that cross a call-count threshold with full optimizations (inlining, loop optimizations), replacing the tier 0 version in the background.

This is RyuJIT's version of C1 → C2: pay almost nothing up front, then spend real compile time only on methods that prove they're worth it. .NET also supports **ReadyToRun**, a hybrid where methods ship pre-JIT-compiled at a baseline quality and RyuJIT can still recompile them better at runtime if they get hot — a middle ground between pure JIT and full AOT.

The CLR ships a generational garbage collector — the mechanics of *why* generational GC works are covered once, in `generational-and-concurrent-gc` (`memory-gc` group), rather than re-derived here. What's CLR-specific worth knowing:

- Three generations (Gen 0, 1, 2) rather than the JVM's typical young/old split, with Gen 0 collected extremely frequently and cheaply.
- A **Large Object Heap (LOH)** for allocations over 85KB, collected separately and less frequently, because large-object compaction is expensive — a CLR-specific design choice with no direct JVM analog.
- Server GC (multi-threaded, throughput-oriented, one heap per core) vs Workstation GC (lower latency, single-threaded) as a top-level mode switch, roughly parallel to the JVM's choice between G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah.

slides.subTitle: Cutting JIT warm-up cost
slides.markdown:
**ReadyToRun (R2R)** precompiles assemblies to native code at build time, storing that native code *alongside* the IL inside the same assembly. At startup, the CLR runs the precompiled native code directly instead of JIT-compiling from IL — cutting the cold-start JIT tax `what-a-runtime-provides` described, especially valuable for CLI tools and serverless functions.

The IL doesn't disappear: RyuJIT can still recompile a method from IL at a higher optimization tier later if it proves hot, so R2R is genuinely a *hybrid*, not a full AOT commitment. .NET also offers full **Native AOT**, which compiles the whole application to a native binary with no IL or JIT at all — the .NET equivalent of `ahead-of-time-compilation-and-native-images`'s GraalVM native-image, trading dynamic features (reflection-heavy code needs explicit support) for the fastest possible start.

slides.sectionTitle: JVM vs CLR, side by side
slides.markdown:
| | JVM | CLR |
|---|---|---|
| Bytecode | Class files, stack-based | IL, stack-based |
| Deployment unit | JAR (bytecode, no built-in rich metadata) | Assembly (IL + self-describing metadata) |
| JIT | C1 (fast) then C2 (aggressive) | Quick JIT (tier 0) then optimized (tier 1) |
| AOT option | GraalVM native-image (separate product) | ReadyToRun (hybrid, built-in) or Native AOT (full) |
| Multi-language story | JVM bytecode target (Kotlin, Scala, Clojure) | First-class: C#, F#, VB.NET share one IL and CLR |
| GC | G1 / ZGC / Shenandoase (pluggable) | Generational, Server/Workstation modes, separate LOH |

The architectures are close enough that a JVM engineer can read CLR internals productively by substitution — the genuine differences are in AOT maturity (built into the .NET toolchain earlier) and metadata richness (assemblies carry more of it natively).

A stale assumption that still costs candidates points: ".NET only runs on Windows, so it's not relevant for cross-platform/cloud-native systems."

That was true of the old .NET Framework. Since .NET Core (now unified simply as "**.NET**", 5 and later), the CLR itself — called **CoreCLR** — is fully cross-platform: Linux, macOS, and Windows, with official Docker images and first-class Kubernetes support. Large-scale services at companies with no Windows infrastructure run .NET on Linux containers today.

The modern honest comparison is JVM vs CLR as two cross-platform managed runtimes with genuinely different language ecosystems and tooling — not "portable JVM vs Windows-locked CLR." Bringing up this history unprompted, correctly, is a good signal in an interview; assuming the old constraint still holds is a real miss.

For `int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;`, `ildasm` or `dotnet-ildasm` shows IL close enough to the JVM bytecode you already read that the pattern should feel familiar:

```
IL_0000: ldarg.1      // push argument 1 (a)
IL_0001: ldarg.2      // push argument 2 (b)
IL_0002: add          // pop two, push their sum
IL_0003: ret           // return top of stack
```

Same shape as the JVM's `iload_1; iload_2; iadd; ireturn` — push, push, operate, return — because IL is stack-based exactly like JVM bytecode. The instruction names differ (`ldarg` vs `iload`) but the mental model transfers directly, which is the whole point of comparing these two runtimes side by side rather than learning the CLR from scratch.

slides.sectionTitle: Compiling C# vs compiling Java, end to end
slides.markdown:
A complete answer to "how is compiling C# different from compiling Java, end to end" should land on: **structurally almost identical, with different names and a more built-in AOT story**.

1. Both compile source to a stack-based intermediate bytecode (IL vs class-file bytecode) via a front-end compiler (Roslyn vs `javac`).
2. Both package that bytecode into a deployable unit carrying metadata (assembly vs JAR — assemblies carry richer metadata natively).
3. Both run on a managed runtime with a tiered JIT (RyuJIT's quick/optimized tiers vs HotSpot's C1/C2) and a generational GC.
4. Both offer an AOT escape hatch for startup-sensitive deployments (ReadyToRun/Native AOT vs GraalVM native-image) — .NET's is more integrated into the mainstream toolchain today.

The honest difference is ecosystem and tooling maturity per use case, not architecture — which is exactly why this topic worked as a compare-and-contrast rather than a fresh introduction.
